items.q: Calculate the mean number of drops held on the coin with 0% soap. Give your answer to one decimal place.
Calculate the median number of drops for the 2% soap water. Give your answer to one decimal place.
The mean for the 2% soap water is 16.75 drops. Which statement best explains why the median describes a typical count for this concentration better than the mean does?
options: One count of 31 is far above the others and pulls the mean upward, while the median stays in the middle of the cluster.
The median is calculated from more of the values than the mean is, so it carries more information about the whole sample of eight counts.
The mean is meant for data sets in which no value repeats, and this set repeats several of its values.
The counts at 2% soap are more tightly clustered than at 0% soap, so a mean exaggerates their center.

items.q: Select ALL statements that are supported by the data in the table.
options: Adding soap lowered the typical number of drops the coin could hold.
The 1% soap data have two modes, 21 and 22 drops.
Removing the 31 from the 2% data would lower the median from 15 to 14 drops.
The range of the 1% data is larger than the range of the 0% data.
The 0% and 1% data overlap: some 1% counts are higher than some 0% counts.

items.q: A student re-checks the 2% notebook and finds the 31 was a copying mistake for 13. After the correction, which describes the change in the mean and the median?
options: The mean drops by 2.25 drops and the median drops by 0.5 drops.
The mean drops by 2.25 drops and the median does not change.
The mean drops by 18 drops and the median drops by 0.5 drops.
The mean and the median both drop by 2.25 drops.

items.q: Calculate the mean cooling time for the 200 g cups. Give your answer in minutes to one decimal place.
Calculate the range of the cooling times for the 200 g cups, in minutes, to one decimal place.
Which statement best describes the data in the table?
options: Doubling the mass of water roughly doubled the typical cooling time, and the 200 g times were more spread out.
Doubling the mass of water roughly doubled the typical cooling time, and the two masses had the same spread.
The 200 g cups cooled faster on average, because their times were more spread out than the 100 g times.
The cooling times are not comparable because each mass was tested in a different set of six cups.

items.q: Which explanation best accounts for the difference in the mean cooling times?
options: Twice the water holds twice the heat at 80 °C, and water releases a lot of heat for each degree it cools, so 200 g takes longer to lose enough heat.
Heavier water molecules form stronger covalent bonds with each other, so the 200 g samples lose heat to the air more slowly.
A larger volume of water has a higher specific heat per gram than a small volume, so each gram of the 200 g sample gives off its heat more slowly.
The 200 g cups evaporate less water, because evaporation happens mainly when water is close to boiling.

items.q: A student records four things about each water sample. Select ALL that are quantitative, continuous data.
options: Temperature of the sample (°C)
Number of drops added (drops)
Color of the dye used (blue, red, green)
Mass of the sample (g)
Whether the sample spilled (yes or no)
Time taken to cool (s)

items.q: Five cups were timed. Four of them took 9.0, 9.4, 8.8 and 9.6 min to cool, and the student's notebook gives the mean of all five as 9.2 min. Calculate the time for the fifth cup, in minutes, to one decimal place.
One of 10 repeat measurements of drops on a coin is 58, while the other nine lie between 27 and 34. What should the student do first?
options: Check the notebook and procedure for a mistake; if none is found, keep the value and report both the mean and the median.
Delete the 58 at once, because a value that does not match the other nine is unlikely to be real data and would distort the summaries of the sample.
Replace the 58 with the mean of the other nine values, so the sample size stays at 10.
Report just the mode, because one unusual value has no effect on the mode.

items.q: A data set of counts is 4, 7, 7, 9, 12. Which change would raise the mean but leave the median and the range unchanged?
options: Changing the 9 to 11
Changing the 12 to 15
Changing the 4 to 6
Changing one 7 to 9

items.q: Group P measured drops on a coin and got 24, 25, 25, 26, 25 (mean 25). Group Q got 18, 31, 25, 22, 29 (mean 25). Which conclusion is best supported?
options: The groups found the same center, but Q's values vary much more, so a single Q measurement is less dependable.
The groups found the same center and the same spread, because their means are equal.
Group Q measured more carefully, because its values cover a wider range of possible counts and so represent more of the possible outcomes.
Group P probably made an error, because real counts of drops rarely repeat so closely.

items.q: Which summary of a data set is found by sorting the values and taking the middle one?
options: Median
Mean
Mode
Midrange

items.q: Put the steps for finding the median of an even-sized data set in order.
options: Sort the values from smallest to largest.
Number the sorted values from 1 to n.
Find the two values in the middle positions (n/2 and n/2 + 1).
Average those two middle values.

items.q: Calculate the slope of the 100 g line between 0 and 5 minutes. Give your answer in °C per minute to one decimal place.
Estimate the temperature of the 100 g sample at 2.5 minutes by reading between the measured points. Give your answer in °C to the nearest whole degree.
A student extends the 100 g line and predicts the water will be at 110 °C after 15 minutes. What is the best evaluation of this prediction?
options: It is unreliable: it extrapolates far past the data, and at normal air pressure liquid water stops warming near 100 °C as heat goes into boiling.
It is reliable, because the points lie on a straight line, and a straight line drawn through data continues at the same slope however far it is extended.
It is unreliable, because the slope should be measured from the 200 g line, which is the larger and more representative sample.
It is reliable, as long as the student uses the slope from the first minute alone, when the hot plate is coldest.

items.q: The slope of the 200 g line is about half the slope of the 100 g line. Which explanation fits?
options: Both hot plates supply heat at the same pace, and twice the mass of water needs twice the heat to rise by each degree.
The 200 g water has a lower specific heat than the 100 g water, so each gram of it warms more slowly when the same heat is supplied.
The 200 g water has fewer hydrogen bonds per gram, so less of the heat it receives is used to warm it up.
The slope of a line depends on how many points are plotted, and both lines were given six points each.

items.q: Which statement best describes the data for the tube with enzyme?
options: Monomer mass rose quickly at first, then rose more and more slowly and leveled off near 50 mg.
Monomer mass rose by the same amount in each 2-minute interval until the end of the run.
Monomer mass rose slowly at first, then rose faster and faster as the run went on.
Monomer mass rose to a peak at 8 minutes and then began to fall as monomers were joined again.

items.q: Calculate the slope of the enzyme curve between 0 and 4 minutes, in mg of monomer per minute, to one decimal place.
Which is the best explanation for why the enzyme curve levels off near 50 mg?
options: The tube started with 50 mg of polymer, so once nearly all of it is broken into monomers there is little left to release.
The enzyme is used up after each reaction it speeds up, so by 10 minutes there is no enzyme left in the tube to break bonds.
Water molecules are used up after 6 minutes, so hydrolysis stops because nothing is left to add across bonds.
The monomers start joining back together by hydrolysis, which balances the breakdown after about 8 minutes.

items.q: What is the purpose of the tube that received water instead of enzyme?
options: It shows how much monomer is released without the enzyme, so the enzyme's effect can be measured against it.
It keeps the volume in both tubes the same, which is its main role in the experiment that was run.
It shows how fast water by itself breaks the enzyme down, so the enzyme dose can be corrected.
It provides extra monomers that the enzyme in the other tube can use to build the polymer again.

items.q: A student measured how much monomer four different enzymes (A, B, C and D) each released from the same polymer in 10 minutes. Which graph type best displays the results?
options: Bar graph, one bar per enzyme
Line graph, joining the four enzymes in order
Histogram of the four masses of monomer released
Scatterplot of enzyme letter against mass released

items.q: A student plans a graph of water temperature (°C) every 30 seconds while a beaker is heated. Select ALL the choices that are correct for this graph.
options: Temperature on the x-axis and time on the y-axis
A line graph, because time is continuous
A bar for each reading, because each reading is a separate category
Axis scales that start at the first and last values recorded, spaced by the readings
Each axis labeled with the quantity and its unit, for example "Time (s)"

items.q: Across 40 lakes, lakes with more plant growth along the shore also had warmer surface water. A student concludes that plant growth warms lakes. What is the best response?
options: The data show a correlation; a third factor, such as more sunlight on shallow lakes, could raise both, so an experiment is needed.
The conclusion is correct, because a strong positive correlation between two measured variables shows that the first variable causes the second one.
The conclusion is backward: the data prove that warm water causes plant growth, since temperature is measured in °C.
The data are useless, because a study of lakes has no independent variable and so it is unable to show a relationship of any kind.

items.q: On a scatterplot of mass of water (g) against time to boil (min) for 12 beakers, the points rise from lower left to upper right and lie close to a straight trend line. What does this show?
options: A strong positive correlation: beakers with more water tended to take longer to boil.
A strong negative correlation: beakers with more water tended to boil sooner.
No correlation, because the points do not touch the trend line exactly.
Each beaker took the same time to boil, because the points form a straight line.

items.q: A student's y-axis for temperature is marked 20, 25, 35, 40, 60 °C at equal spacing, one mark for each reading she took. What is wrong, and what does it do to the graph?
options: The scale is uneven, so equal distances stand for different temperature changes and the shape of the curve is distorted.
Nothing is wrong, because each recorded value appears on the axis, so a reader can find the exact temperature of each point.
The scale should start at 0 °C; any axis that starts above zero is an error.
The temperatures should be on the x-axis, because they are the numbers that were recorded.

items.q: A student measures the mass of 60 seeds and wants to show how many seeds fall in each 0.1 g range. Which graph type is this?
options: Histogram
Line graph
Scatterplot
Pie chart of seed masses

items.q: Put the steps for building a graph from a data table in order.
options: Decide which variable is independent and which is dependent.
Choose the graph type from the kind of independent variable.
Draw and label the axes with quantities and units, using even scales that fit the data.
Plot the points or bars for each group.
Add a key for the groups and a title, and draw a trend line if one is needed.

items.q: A trend line on a graph of monomer released (mg) against time (min) passes through (3, 14) and (9, 41). Calculate its slope in mg per minute, to one decimal place.
Calculate the standard deviation of the set times at 85 °C. Give your answer in seconds to one decimal place.
Calculate the standard error of the mean set time at 75 °C. Give your answer in seconds to one decimal place.
Which statement best describes the variability in these data?
options: The standard deviation is largest at 65 °C, but compared with each mean, the spread is similar at all three temperatures.
The 65 °C eggs were handled least carefully, because their standard deviation is about eight times the value measured at 85 °C.
The spread is identical at the three temperatures, because each row contains exactly five eggs.
The 85 °C data are the most variable, because their mean is the smallest of the three temperatures tested.

items.q: Which explanation best accounts for the trend in the mean set times?
options: At higher temperatures molecules move faster, so the proteins' folds are shaken apart sooner and the unfolded chains tangle sooner.
At higher temperatures new peptide bonds form between the amino acids, linking neighboring proteins into a firm solid more quickly.
At higher temperatures the water evaporates from the tubes faster, so the egg white dries out and turns firm and white.
At higher temperatures the proteins gain extra amino acids from the water, so their primary structure changes faster.

items.q: The two cereals have nearly the same mean protein content. What do the standard deviations show?
options: Cereal B varies far more from box to box, so a single box of B is a less dependable guide to its protein content.
Cereal B contains more protein than cereal A, because a larger standard deviation means larger values overall.
Cereal A was measured less precisely, because its standard deviation is close to zero and so tells us little.
The two cereals are identical, because standard deviation does not matter when the means are the same.

items.q: Calculate the standard error of the mean for cereal B. Give your answer in g/100 g to two decimal places.
The lab wants the standard error for cereal B to be about 0.36 g/100 g instead of about 0.71. Assuming the standard deviation stays near 1.75, how many boxes should it test?
options: About 24 boxes, four times as many
About 12 boxes, twice as many
About 3 boxes, half as many
About 36 boxes, six times as many

items.q: If the lab tested 60 boxes of cereal B instead of 6, what would most likely happen to the standard deviation and the standard error?
options: The standard deviation would stay about the same, and the standard error would get much smaller.
Both the standard deviation and the standard error would get much smaller, by about the same factor.
The standard deviation would get much smaller, and the standard error would stay about the same.
Both would get larger, because more boxes give more chances for unusual values to appear.

items.q: In a normal distribution, about what percentage of values fall within 2 standard deviations of the mean?
Five 100 g samples of lentils contained 11, 13, 14, 15 and 17 g of protein. Calculate the standard deviation in grams, to two decimal places.
A student calculating a standard deviation from 5 values divides the sum of squared deviations by 5 instead of 4. How does her answer compare with the correct value?
options: It is a little too small, because dividing by n instead of n − 1 gives a smaller result.
It is a little too large, because dividing by a larger number makes the answer larger.
It is the same, because n and n − 1 differ by just 1, which has no effect on the square root.
It is too small by a factor of 5, because each squared deviation was divided by an extra 5.

items.q: Two sets of five measurements have the same mean of 50 g. Set X: 49, 50, 50, 50, 51. Set Y: 40, 45, 50, 55, 60. Without calculating, which is true?
options: Set Y has the larger standard deviation, because its values sit farther from the mean.
The two sets have the same standard deviation, because they have the same mean.
Set X has the larger standard deviation, because more of its values equal the mean.
Neither set has a standard deviation, because five values are too few to calculate one.

items.q: A student says: "The standard error is smaller than the standard deviation, so it is a better measure of how variable my eggs were." What is the best response?
options: SD describes how much individual eggs varied; SE describes how precisely the mean is known, so they answer different questions.
The student is right, because a smaller number shows that the measurements were more precise, so it is the better one to report for eggs.
Standard error is larger than standard deviation for small samples, so the student has made a calculation mistake.
The two are the same quantity written two ways, so it makes no difference which one is used.

items.q: Put the steps for calculating the standard error of the mean in order.
options: Calculate the mean, x̄.
Subtract the mean from each value and square each result.
Add the squares and divide by n − 1.
Take the square root to get s.
Divide s by √n.

items.q: The student adds a sixth egg at 85 °C that sets in 61 s. What happens to the mean and the standard deviation?
options: The mean drops slightly and the standard deviation drops slightly, because 61 s is close to the mean.
The mean stays at 62 s and the standard deviation rises, because adding any value adds spread.
The mean drops by 1 s and the standard deviation stays at 3.2 s, because the mean depends on n and the SD does not.
Both stay the same, because a single value has too small an effect to change either statistic.

items.q: Calculate the average rate at which the color moved into the cube over the whole 10 minutes, in mm per minute, to two decimal places.
Calculate the average rate between 8 and 10 minutes, in mm per minute, to two decimal places.
Which statement best describes how the rate of color movement changed during the experiment?
options: The rate was highest in the first 2 minutes (0.8 mm/min) and then fell, to 0.2 mm/min in each of the last two intervals.
The rate stayed at 0.36 mm/min throughout, because that is the average rate for the whole run of the experiment.
The rate increased over time, because the depth of color was greatest at 10 minutes, the end of the run.
The rate fell to zero after 8 minutes, because the curve flattened out and the color stopped moving into the agar.

items.q: Which explanation best accounts for the falling rate?
options: As the color moves deeper, the concentration difference is spread over a longer distance, so the gradient driving diffusion is less steep.
The colored molecules get larger as they move into the agar, so each one moves more slowly than it did when it first entered at the surface.
The agar cube grows larger as it absorbs the solution, so the color has a bigger volume to fill as time goes on.
The solution outside the cube runs out of colored molecules after 2 minutes, so diffusion slows to a steady trickle.

items.q: Calculate the percent change in the rate of color movement from the 0-2 minute interval to the 8-10 minute interval. Give your answer to the nearest whole percent (use a minus sign for a decrease).
Calculate the surface area : volume ratio of the 3 cm cube, in cm⁻¹, to one decimal place.
From the 1 cm cube to the 3 cm cube, the volume colored fell from 97.8% to 56.1%. Which description is correct?
options: A fall of 41.7 percentage points, which is a 42.6% decrease relative to the 1 cm cube.
A fall of 41.7 percentage points, which is the same thing as a 41.7% decrease.
A 42.6% decrease, which is the same thing as a fall of 42.6 percentage points.
A 74.3% decrease, because 41.7 is 74.3% of the 3 cm cube's value of 56.1.

items.q: Which claim do these data best support?
options: As a cube gets larger its SA : V ratio falls, so a smaller share of its volume is reached by diffusion in a given time.
Larger cubes take up color faster, because their larger surface area lets more color in per minute in total across their six faces.
The color moved deeper into the larger cubes, which is why their percentage of colored volume came out lower.
Cube size does not affect diffusion, because the color reached the same depth of 3.6 mm in each cube.

items.q: A single cell depends on diffusion across its surface for supplies. Based on the cube data, what would doubling the cell's side length (keeping its shape) do?
options: Halve its surface area : volume ratio, so each unit of volume would get about half as much surface for exchange.
Double its surface area : volume ratio, because both the surface area and the volume would increase.
Leave its surface area : volume ratio unchanged, because the cell would keep exactly the same shape.
Quarter its surface area : volume ratio, because volume grows with the square of the side length while area stays the same.

items.q: Root hairs raise the surface area of a seedling's root from 40 cm² to 130 cm². Calculate the percent increase, to the nearest whole percent.
A bacterium is 2 µm long. What is its length in millimeters?
options: 2 × 10³ mm

items.q: A cube-shaped cell is 10 µm on each side. What is its volume in cubic millimeters?
options: 1 × 10⁻⁶ mm³
1 × 10⁻³ mm³
1 × 10⁻² mm³
1 × 10³ mm³

items.q: A 1-liter flask of water cooled from 80 °C to 52 °C in 14 minutes. Calculate the average rate of cooling, in °C per minute, to one decimal place.
A 100 mL flask and a 1,000 mL flask of the same shape, both at 80 °C, are left in the same room. Which prediction about their average cooling rates over the first 10 minutes is best supported?
options: The 100 mL flask cools faster, because it has more surface per unit volume through which heat can leave.
The 1,000 mL flask cools faster, because its larger surface area loses more heat in total each minute.
Both cool at the same rate, because water has the same specific heat whatever the amount.
The 1,000 mL flask cools faster, because a larger mass of water holds its heat for less time.

items.q: A culture of 400 bacteria falls by 50% after an antibiotic is added, then rises by 50% after the antibiotic is removed. How many bacteria are there at the end?
On a curved graph of product made against time, the curve is steep at first and then flattens. Select ALL statements that are true.
options: The instantaneous rate is highest near the start.
The average rate over the whole run equals the rate at the start.
The average rate over the run is the slope of a straight line joining the first and last points.
The instantaneous rate rises as the curve flattens.
The rate in any interval is the amount made multiplied by the time it took.

items.q: Select ALL pairs of temperatures whose means are likely different, based on the error bars.
options: 20 °C and 40 °C
40 °C and 60 °C
60 °C and 70 °C
20 °C and 70 °C

items.q: The 70 °C mean is 0.16 higher than the 60 °C mean. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: The data do not show a difference between 60 °C and 70 °C, because the error bars overlap; a larger sample might reveal one.
Heating to 70 °C caused more leakage than 60 °C, because the 70 °C mean is higher by 0.16 absorbance units.
Heating to 70 °C caused the same leakage as 60 °C, because overlapping error bars prove the means are equal.
No conclusion is possible about any of the temperatures, because the 70 °C error bar is the widest of the four bars on the graph.

items.q: The 70 °C error bar is ± 0.12 and represents ± 2SE. With n = 8, what is the standard deviation of the 70 °C absorbances? Give your answer to two decimal places.
Which explanation best accounts for the large increase in leakage between 40 °C and 60 °C?
options: Above about 40 °C, heat disrupts the bilayer and denatures membrane proteins, so the membrane stops being a selective barrier.
Above 40 °C, the red substance becomes small and nonpolar, so it passes through an intact bilayer by simple diffusion.
Above 40 °C, aquaporins open wider and let the red substance pass through them along with the water molecules.
Above 40 °C, the cell walls dissolve, and the cell wall is the structure that keeps the red substance in the cell.

items.q: Why is the 70 °C error bar wider than the 20 °C error bar?
options: The 70 °C cubes varied more from one another, so the standard error of their mean is larger.
More cubes were tested at 70 °C, and testing more cubes tends to make an error bar wider.
The 70 °C mean is larger, and a larger mean comes with a proportionally wider error bar.
Error bars get wider as temperature rises, whatever the data, because heat adds uncertainty.

items.q: Calculate the standard error of the mean at 25 °C, in µm²/s, to two decimal places.
Calculate the upper limit of the 95% confidence interval (x̄ + 2SE) for the 15 °C mean, in µm²/s, to one decimal place.
Using 95% confidence intervals (x̄ ± 2SE), which comparison shows a likely real difference?
options: 15 °C and 25 °C: the intervals 1.6-2.0 and 2.26-2.74 do not overlap.
25 °C and 35 °C: the 35 °C mean is 0.5 higher than the 25 °C mean.
Both comparisons, because fluidity rises steadily from each temperature to the next.
Neither comparison, because the 35 °C group has fewer membranes than the other groups.

items.q: The researchers suspect fluidity really is higher at 35 °C than at 25 °C. What change to the experiment would best test this?
options: Test more membranes at 35 °C, which shrinks its standard error and narrows its confidence interval.
Report the standard deviation instead of the confidence interval, because it does not depend on n.
Remove the lowest 35 °C value so the mean rises and the interval moves away from the 25 °C one.
Raise the temperature to 45 °C, so that the difference from 25 °C becomes large enough to see clearly.

items.q: For the exam, how is an approximate 95% confidence interval for a mean calculated?
options: Mean ± 2 standard errors
Mean ± 2 standard deviations
Mean ± 1 standard error
Mean ± the range ÷ 2

items.q: A graph shows two bars with error bars that do not overlap, but the caption does not say what the error bars represent. What is the best response?
options: Ask what the bars show, because non-overlapping SD or SE bars mean something different from non-overlapping 95% CI bars.
Conclude the means differ, because non-overlapping error bars of any kind show a real difference.
Conclude the means do not differ, because error bars that are not labeled are usually standard deviations.
Ignore the error bars and compare just the heights of the two bars, which is what the means are.

items.q: In an experiment on how a substance affects leakage from beet cells, the 95% CI error bars of the treated and untreated groups do not overlap. Which conclusion is worded best?
options: The difference is statistically significant, so we reject the null hypothesis that the substance has no effect on leakage.
The substance has been proved to cause leakage, so the alternative hypothesis is now known to be true for beet cells in general.
The difference is due to chance, because the two groups were made of different beet cubes.
The null hypothesis is accepted, because the error bars show where the true means lie.

items.q: Sixteen beet cubes gave a mean absorbance of 0.40 with a standard deviation of 0.08. Calculate the lower limit of the 95% confidence interval (x̄ − 2SE), to two decimal places.
Group P: mean 5.0, 95% CI 4.6-5.4. Group Q: mean 5.5, 95% CI 5.3-5.7. A student says, "The bars overlap, so the treatment had no effect." What is the best evaluation?
options: Too strong: overlap means the data do not show a difference, not that there is none; overlapping 95% CIs can still hide a real one.
Correct: overlapping 95% confidence intervals prove that the two population means are equal.
Incorrect: Q's interval is narrower, so Q's data are more reliable, and its higher mean therefore shows a clear effect of the treatment.
Incorrect: the means differ by 0.5, which is larger than the width of Q's interval, so they differ.

items.q: Which change makes a 95% confidence interval narrower?
options: Measuring more individuals
Measuring fewer individuals
Reporting ± 2 SD instead of ± 2 SE
Rounding the mean to fewer decimal places

items.q: Put the steps for comparing two group means with 95% confidence intervals in order.
options: Calculate the mean and standard deviation of each group.
Calculate each group's standard error, SE = s ÷ √n.
Calculate each interval as mean ± 2SE.
Check whether the two intervals overlap.
Decide whether to reject the null hypothesis of no difference.

items.q: Estimate the sucrose concentration at which the potato cores would neither gain nor lose mass. Give your answer in mol/L to two decimal places.
Calculate the solute potential of a 0.30 mol/L sucrose solution at 22 °C. Give your answer in bars to one decimal place.
What does the concentration where the cores neither gain nor lose mass tell you?
options: At that concentration the solution's water potential equals the potato cells' water potential, so there is no net water movement.
At that concentration the potato cells contain exactly 0.30 mol/L of sucrose, the same as the surrounding solution in the beaker.
At that concentration water stops crossing the membranes in either direction, because the aquaporins close.
At that concentration the cores are plasmolyzed, so they can no longer take in or lose water by osmosis.

items.q: Why did the cores in 0.8 mol/L sucrose lose mass?
options: The solution had a lower (more negative) water potential than the cells, so water moved out of the cells by osmosis.
Sucrose moved into the cells by diffusion and pushed water out, so the cores became lighter as a result.
The solution had a higher water potential than the cells, so water moved from the solution into the cells.
The high sucrose concentration dissolved part of the potato cell walls, so the cores lost solid mass.

items.q: Why did the students record percent change in mass rather than change in grams?
options: The cores did not all start at the same mass, and percent change lets cores of different sizes be compared fairly.
Percent change turns losses into positive numbers, which makes a graph of the results easier to read and compare.
Change in grams would be the same for each core, so it would not show any effect of sucrose concentration.
The balance could weigh just in percent, so grams were converted to percent for the final report.

items.q: Calculate the solute potential of the 0.1 mol/L NaCl solution at 25 °C. Give your answer in bars to two decimal places.
Why does the CaCl₂ solution have three times the solute potential magnitude of the sucrose solution at the same molar concentration?
options: Each CaCl₂ unit dissolves into three particles (Ca²⁺ and two Cl⁻), and solute potential depends on the number of dissolved particles.
CaCl₂ molecules are about three times heavier than sucrose molecules, so each one lowers the water potential of the solution three times as much.
Calcium ions carry a charge of 2+, and solute potential depends on the charge on each dissolved particle.
CaCl₂ binds three times as many water molecules into covalent bonds, removing them from the solution.

items.q: A bag made of membrane that lets water through but not sucrose or ions is filled with the 0.1 mol/L sucrose solution and placed in a beaker of the 0.1 mol/L NaCl solution. What happens?
options: Water leaves the bag, because the NaCl solution's water potential (−4.95 bars) is lower than the sucrose solution's (−2.48 bars).
Water enters the bag, because sucrose molecules are larger than ions and attract more water molecules to them.
Nothing happens, because the two solutions have the same molar concentration of solute, 0.1 mol/L each, on both sides of the bag.
Sodium and chloride ions enter the bag until both sides have equal numbers of dissolved particles.

items.q: Select ALL solutions that would have the same water potential as the 0.1 mol/L NaCl solution at 25 °C in an open beaker.
options: 0.2 mol/L sucrose
0.1 mol/L glucose
0.05 mol/L NaCl
0.2 mol/L CaCl₂
0.3 mol/L sucrose

items.q: A plant cell has a solute potential of −9.0 bars and a pressure potential of +3.0 bars. Calculate its water potential in bars, to one decimal place.
A plant cell with Ψs = −9.0 bars and ΨP = +3.0 bars (Ψ = −6.0 bars) is placed in a large beaker of 0.3 mol/L sucrose at 22 °C (Ψ ≈ −7.4 bars). What happens to the cell?
options: It loses water, so its pressure potential falls as its turgor drops.
It gains water, so its pressure potential rises as it becomes more turgid.
It neither gains nor loses water, because its solute potential is more negative than the solution's.
It gains sucrose, so its solute potential becomes less negative over time.

items.q: Calculate the solute potential of a 0.5 mol/L sucrose solution at 27 °C. Give your answer in bars to one decimal place.
A student calculates the solute potential of 0.30 mol/L sucrose at 22 °C but uses T = 22 instead of 295. How does her answer compare with the correct value?
options: It is about 13 times too close to zero (−0.55 instead of −7.4 bars).
It is about 13 times too negative (−98 instead of −7.4 bars).
It is the same, because temperature units cancel in the equation.
It has the wrong sign, because Celsius temperatures can be negative.

items.q: A solution has a water potential of −7.4 bars. What is this in megapascals (MPa)?
options: −74 MPa
−7.4 MPa

items.q: For a solution in an open beaker, why is its water potential equal to its solute potential?
options: An open beaker puts no extra pressure on the solution, so its pressure potential is 0.
An open beaker lets solutes evaporate, so the solute potential becomes the one potential left.
In an open beaker the solute potential is 0, so the pressure potential is what counts.
Water potential is defined as solute potential whenever the temperature is held constant.

items.q: Put the steps for finding the water potential of a solution in an open beaker in order.
options: Find i (1 for sucrose, about 2 for NaCl) and C in mol/L.
Convert the temperature to kelvin: °C + 273.
Calculate Ψs = −iCRT with R = 0.0831 L·bar/(mol·K).
Add ΨP, which is 0 for an open container, to get Ψ.
Compare Ψ values: water moves toward the more negative one.

items.q: What is the null hypothesis for this experiment?
options: Pill bugs show no preference, so they will be split equally between the moist and dry sides.
Pill bugs prefer the moist side, so more than half of them will be found on that side of the chamber.
Pill bugs prefer the dry side, because dry conditions keep their bodies at a steady temperature.
The number of pill bugs on the moist side depends on how many are on the dry side of the chamber.

items.q: Calculate the chi-square value. Give your answer to one decimal place.
Which conclusion follows from the chi-square test at p = 0.05?
options: χ² = 8.1 is greater than 3.84 (df = 1), so reject the null hypothesis: the split is unlikely to be chance.
χ² = 8.1 is greater than 3.84 (df = 1), so fail to reject the null hypothesis: the bugs show no preference.
χ² = 8.1 is less than 9.49 (df = 4), so fail to reject the null hypothesis, because the 40 bugs are the categories.
χ² = 8.1 is greater than 0.05, so reject the null hypothesis, because any χ² above 0.05 is significant.

items.q: Pill bugs breathe through gill-like structures that must stay moist. Which statement best connects the result to biology?
options: Animals that move toward moist places lose less water from their breathing surfaces, which fits the strong preference for the moist side.
The chi-square test shows that moisture causes pill bugs to live longer, because more of them were found alive on the moist side.
The test proves that pill bugs choose the moist side on purpose, because they want to keep their breathing surfaces wet.
The result shows that dry air damages the pill bugs' membranes, because the 11 bugs on the dry side had stopped moving.

items.q: The student repeats the test, but this time the moist side sits under a lamp. Why would this weaken her conclusion about moisture?
options: Light and heat would now differ between sides along with moisture, so a preference could not be credited to moisture alone.
A lamp would make the pill bugs move faster, which would lower the total number counted to fewer than 40.
Under a lamp the expected values would change from 20 and 20 to 30 and 10, which the chi-square test is not designed to handle.
The chi-square test is meant for experiments done in the dark, because light adds random error to the counts of animals.

items.q: How many degrees of freedom does this test have?
Calculate the chi-square value for the null hypothesis that the pill bugs spread equally among the four sections. Give your answer to two decimal places.
Which statement about the test is correct?
options: The null hypothesis is rejected at p = 0.05 (8.13 > 7.82) but not at p = 0.01 (8.13 < 11.34).
The null hypothesis is rejected at both p = 0.05 and p = 0.01, because 8.13 is larger than 3.84.
The null hypothesis is not rejected at either level, because 8.13 is less than 9.49, the value for 4 sections.
The null hypothesis is rejected at p = 0.01 but not at p = 0.05, because the stricter level is easier to pass.

items.q: Which section contributed most to the chi-square value, and what does that suggest?
options: Dark and moist (5.40 of 8.13): far more bugs gathered there than chance predicts.
Light and dry (2.40 of 8.13): far fewer bugs went there than in any other section of the chamber.
Dark and dry (0.07 of 8.13): its count was closest to expected, so it drives the result.
Each section contributed equally, because the expected value was 15 in each of the sections.

items.q: A seed company says its packet grows equal numbers of red- and white-flowered plants. A student grows 100 plants: 54 red and 46 white. Calculate χ² to two decimal places.
For the seed packet (χ² = 0.64, df = 1, critical value 3.84 at p = 0.05), which conclusion is correct?
options: Fail to reject the null hypothesis: the 54 : 46 split is consistent with chance around a 1 : 1 ratio.
Reject the null hypothesis: 54 is more than 50, so the packet holds more red seeds than claimed.
Accept the null hypothesis: the test proves the packet contains exactly equal numbers of each.
Reject the null hypothesis: a χ² that is less than 3.84 means the data differ from what was expected.

items.q: A test gives p = 0.03. Which interpretation is correct?
options: If the null hypothesis were true, a deviation this large or larger would occur about 3% of the time.
There is a 3% chance that the alternative hypothesis is true, so the alternative is very unlikely.
There is a 97% chance that the experiment was done correctly and its results can be trusted.
The observed values differ from the expected values by about 3% of the total count in the experiment.

items.q: A student enters percentages (moist 72.5%, dry 27.5%) instead of counts into the chi-square formula. Why is this a mistake?
options: χ² depends on sample size: a 72.5 : 27.5 split from 400 animals is stronger evidence than from 40, and percentages hide that.
Percentages add up to 100, so the expected values are not possible to calculate from them in the usual way for the two sides.
Percentages should not be squared, because squaring a percentage gives units that have no meaning in biology.
Percentages make χ² smaller in most cases, so a real difference would usually be missed by the test.

items.q: Researchers expect birds to use three feeders in the ratio 50% : 30% : 20% (by feeder size). They record 200 visits: 86, 74 and 40. Calculate χ² to two decimal places.
In a chi-square test, what is the critical value?
options: The table value, for the degrees of freedom and significance level, that χ² has to exceed to reject the null
The largest observed count among the categories, which sets the scale for each of the other terms in the sum
The sum of the expected values, which has to equal the total number of individuals counted in the study
The probability that the null hypothesis is true, read from the bottom row of the table

items.q: Put the steps of a chi-square goodness-of-fit test in order.
options: State the null hypothesis and the split it predicts.
Calculate the expected count for each category from the total.
Calculate (o − e)² ÷ e for each category and add them to get χ².
Find df = number of categories − 1 and the critical value at p = 0.05.
Compare χ² with the critical value and decide whether to reject the null.
